rss_0_1791850896.title: Award-winning microscopy image disqualified over AI use
rss_0_1791850896.text:
A winning video showing beating airway cilia has been disqualified from the Small World in Motion competition for failing to comply with competition rules.Credit: Ning Xu/Nikon Small World

The winning entry of the prestigious Small World in Motion microscopy competition has been disqualified after scientists raised concerns about its creation using artificial intelligence.

On 9 October, Nikon Instruments, which runs the competition, said in a statement that the winning video did not comply with competition rules. AI-generated videos are not permitted, according to the competition website.

The video was submitted by Ning Xu, an optical engineer at the National University of Singapore. It showed the movement of hair-like structures called cilia in the lungs and was awarded first place on 15 September. But in days, scientists noted on social-media platform LinkedIn that some features in the video seemed biologically implausible.

In response to those comments, Xu wrote on LinkedIn that his team had used an AI model in post-processing to enhance the visual presentation of the regions below the cilia “without making anatomical claims about what those rendered features represent”. These posts, which appeared under Nikon’s earlier announcement on LinkedIn that Xu had won the prize, have since been taken down.

On 25 September, a Nikon Small World spokesperson told Nature that the company was investigating the video. In its latest statement, Nikon Instruments said that after re-evaluating the video and supporting materials, and consulting the judging panel, it determined that the winning video did not comply with the competition rules. “This decision is based solely on the submitted video’s eligibility under the rules outlined for this competition. It should not be interpreted as a judgment of the entrant’s professional reputation, scientific contributions, or intent,” the company said.

Xu did not respond to Nature’s request for comment about Nikon’s decision to disqualify his entry. A spokesperson for the National University of Singapore said Ning Xu participated in the competition before he joined the university and the content of his submission is unrelated to his work there.

rss_2_1791850899.title: Keep medical doctors in academia — without them, health-care research will suffer
rss_2_1791850899.text:
Physician-scientists are well placed to do translational and clinical research.Credit: Janiec Bros/Getty

Medical doctors who also do research are an increasingly rare breed. Physician-scientists made up nearly 5% of the US medical workforce in the 1980s; today, that figure is closer to 1.5%1. In the United Kingdom, the proportion of senior doctors working as academics fell from almost 5% in 2009 to roughly 3% in 2025 (see ‘Physician-scientists on the ropes’), with the number of physician-scientists under the age of 36 plunging by a whopping 25% between 2024 and 2025 (see go.nature.com/4ygjfev). In Japan, 2.1% of all doctors were physician-scientists in 1996; this proportion dropped to 1.6% in 2016. Moreover, the number of physician-scientists aged 39 or younger halved in the same period2.

Whistleblowing in science: this physician faced ostracization after standing up to pharma

Underlying the decline is an inability to retain young physician-scientists at a high enough rate to replace senior professionals as they retire. Around the world, clinical academics describe funding instability and a lack of career support as barriers to staying in their posts3–6. In the United States, according to a survey posted on the preprint website medRxiv, more than half of early-career physician-scientists are considering quitting their academic duties to pursue a purely clinical career7. That’s markedly higher than the 31% of US physicians who report considering leaving their current post within two years.

This trend is alarming because physician-scientists are hugely valuable for health-care research. Their expertise makes them ideally placed to pioneer advances in translational medicine, formulate and run medical trials to improve clinical practice, and drive economic growth. More than one-third of the Nobel Prizes in Physiology or Medicine and Lasker Awards for basic science have been awarded to physician-scientists8.

South Korea offers a glimpse of what is at stake. The number of medical research papers it published was already declining — probably owing to funding cuts — when, in 2024, mass resignations by resident physicians forced physician-scientists to abandon research to cover clinical duties9. That year, publications fell by 12%, roughly double the decline in the previous year, presumably in part because of the lack of papers from physician-scientists.

Our own experiences have further convinced us of the value of this group. Two of us (R.M. and R.B.) currently lead the University College London MB–PhD programme, which has run since 1994. It enables undergraduate medical students to undertake a PhD in scientific research, typically between their fourth and fifth years — one of several routes to becoming a physician-scientist. Papers authored by our cohort of 131 graduates from the programme between 1994 and 2026 received about three times as many citations each per year as did comparable papers in related fields10.

These results are just a snapshot from a small group, and there are many factors that could contribute to the cohort’s high performance. However, we think that they highlight the importance of the blended expertise that defines physician-scientists.

That expertise is now eroding around the world. Governments, funders, universities and others must take urgent steps to stop the decline.

Reasons for the drop-off

In many countries, medical graduates are matched to their first postgraduate positions by centralized, algorithmic systems built for all physicians. These systems do not always consider research potential. In England, for instance, two-thirds of posts historically reserved for aspiring physician-scientists are now allocated by an algorithm that does not take into account publication record11. When recruitment processes consider research, they often reward the quantity of a candidate’s research output rather than quality.

Long COVID still has no cure — so these patients are turning to research

There’s no guarantee that the location to which a physician-scientist is recruited will have an academic department nearby where they can pursue their research area of interest. Schemes implemented in countries such as the United Kingdom, Australia and Canada deliberately post doctors to under-served regions. This is a sensible response to genuine workforce shortages, but one that can inadvertently displace physician-scientists far away from the infrastructure that their research depends on.

Next, there’s a lack of career support. Once a physician-scientist is in a post, health systems often fail to dedicate time and support for research. They might be awarded protected research time on paper but spend it covering rota gaps or absorbing high clinical workloads. One UK survey found that more than 50% of physicians reported a lack of protected research time in their job plans12. Mentoring is often lacking13, and when it’s available, it might not come from people who understand both the clinical and scientific sides of the job.

Strong mentorship could help junior physician-scientists to navigate a tricky career path.Credit: Lu ShaoJi/Getty

Pay for physician-scientists often falls short of that for equivalent, purely clinical posts. In the United States, for example, academic physicians are compensated, on average, about US$50,000 less per year than are conventional hospital doctors (see go.nature.com/4y9anls). The same problem occurs across Europe3. And in England, although a pay premium recognizes physicians who combine research with clinical training, some people are ineligible — notably, those who receive a PhD before graduating in medicine.

Underpinning all of these challenges is funding instability, in both medicine and research. In 2025, US federal funding cuts forced universities to rescind offers already made to incoming physician–PhD (MD–PhD) students. The Canadian Institutes of Health Research announced that it would revoke funding for its national MD–PhD training programme in 2015 and has yet to replace it. In the past few years, research funding has been cut in countries including Argentina and the Netherlands14, resulting in fewer grants and fewer researchers.

Rebuild the workforce

A coordinated effort from governments, funders, health systems, universities and physician-scientists is needed to retain more people in this profession.

Health and science ministries should track how many doctors at each career stage enter fundamental or clinical research, remain active or leave. They should publish where and why attrition occurs. This will let ministries target interventions at the points at which talent is lost and assess whether reforms are working.

rss_3_1791850901.title: Economics Nobel awarded for work on stabilizing economies in crisis
rss_3_1791850901.text:
Credit: Jonathan Nackstrand/AFP via Getty

The 2026 Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel has been awarded to economists Robert E. Hall and Michael Woodford for their research on how to stabilize an economy to avoid socially and economically damaging fluctuations in inflation, growth and employment.

The work, in the words of the prize awarding committee, “generated a paradigm shift in stabilisation policy and [is] now used by central banks and finance ministries around the world”.

“This is an excellent prize, honouring two superb and highly influential economists,” says economist John Cochrane of the Hoover Institution, a thinktank based at Stanford University. Olivier Blanchard, formerly chief economist at the International Monetary Fund, says the laureates have “dramatically changed the conduct of monetary policy”.

According to Cochrane, there were “a dozen plausible contenders at least” to share a prize in this field. “I would hate to be the Nobel Prize committee deciding which two or three to recognize”, he says, but “Hall and Woodford were top contenders on anyone’s list”.

Speaking by phone during the prize announcement, Woodford said he was “elated” by the award. He added that his theory was intended not just to guide policy but also to help governments explain to the public why they make economic interventions in the way they do, “to talk to people about why the things that are being done are being done”.

“Together, Hall’s and Woodford’s contributions amount to a new foundation for the theory of macroeconomic fluctuations”, say the Nobel committee, “allowing us to obtain a deeper understanding of the sources and propagation mechanisms behind recessions and booms.”

The return of Keynes

The work of the two laureates, who share the prize of 12 million Swedish kronor (around $1.2 million), builds on the ideas of the twentieth century British economist John Maynard Keynes.

Credit: Tim Gidal/Picture Post/Hulton Archive/Getty

Keynes argued that governments need to intervene on a big scale in times of economic instability to avoid crashes and mass unemployment as happened in the Great Depression of the 1930s. Market forces alone cannot give an economy sufficient agility to respond to such crises, he contended in books such as How to Pay for the War, published just after Britain had declared war against Nazi Germany (Macmillan, 1940).

Keynes’ ideas became highly influential from the mid-20th-century onwards. They were relevant as recently as the COVID-19 pandemic when governments around the world funded businesses so they could retain their staff during lockdowns. But these ideas did not prevent the rollercoaster of economic boom and bust, evident for example in the oil crisis of the 1970s, and the financial crisis of 2008.

Hall and Woodford effect

Hall and Woodford’s work has helped to explain what was missing in Keynes’ macroeconomic picture – the study of the economy as a whole – by diving deep into the microeconomic perspective, which considers how decisions made by individual businesses and households affect prices, earnings, and spending.

Hall, based at Stanford University in California, recognized that people’s decisions about consumption depend not just on quantifiable factors such as earnings but on what Keynes himself called “animal spirits”: psychological factors that drive economic choices, in this case expectations about the future.

In two key papers, in 1978 and in 1982, Hall showed that it is possible to estimate the proportion of spenders who take a rational view of how they think future monetary and fiscal policies might change, as well as those who in contrast make their decisions about consumption based only on an immediate, gloomy prospect of having no savings or access to borrowing. In effect, this amounts to estimating the proportions of the population that are forward-looking in their spending decisions and that are not. Hall validated his predictions against real-world data on consumption.

Woodford, based at Columbia University in New York, built on such work about expectations to create a 'New Keynesian' microeconomic theory, which culminated in his book Interest and Prices: Foundations of a Theory of Monetary Policy (Princeton University Press, 2003).

rss_4_1791850902.title: Beyond the solvent fog: watching molecules dance in the crowd
rss_4_1791850902.text:
One of the greatest challenges in modern physical chemistry — monitoring how molecules behave, interact and transform in a crowded liquid environment — seems simple, yet is anything but. Writing in Nature, Kim et al.1 apply the technique of time-resolved X-ray liquidography to the study of a textbook chemical reaction — the light-induced rearrangement of atoms in azobenzene molecules in solution. In doing so, the authors reveal details of this photoisomerization process and demonstrate the technique’s utility for studying low-mass atoms in a bulky solvent.

Nature 658, 613-615 (2026)

rss_5_1791850904.title: What does a PhD pay? Data reveal huge gaps across Europe
rss_5_1791850904.text:
Denmark and other Scandinavian countries are seen as top destinations for PhD candidates from other European nations.Credit: Bumble Dee/Shutterstock

How much do PhD students earn? The first comprehensive overview of PhD income shows vast imbalances across much of Europe1.

The report, which investigated the earnings of first-year doctoral candidates in 2024–25 across 26 countries, was published by the European Council of Doctoral Candidates and Junior Researchers (Eurodoc) in September.

“Collecting comparative data on remuneration across Europe is notoriously difficult,” says Norbert Bencze, one of the authors of the report and president of Eurodoc — an international federation based in Brussels that represents early-career researchers and doctoral candidates across Europe. “Our aim is to draw attention to the disparities, and to encourage more data collection.”

Co-author Pil Maria Saugmann, an academic governance researcher and former Eurodoc president, says that these figures contribute to a “brain drain” directed towards Scandinavia and the Benelux countries from many other parts of Europe (see ‘Is it a job?’).

Source: Ref. 1

But Estonia has shown that it is possible to buck that trend, Saugmann adds. A 2022 doctoral education reform replaced a student stipend of around €8,000 (about US$9,000) a year with a guaranteed salary of about 2.5 times that amount, boosting applications for doctoral positions, as well as connections to industry, she says.

Accounting complexities

Remuneration schemes can be difficult to compare, says Bencze. Some doctoral candidates are employed with salaries, others are on scholarships and some have mixed arrangements. The cost of living, which differs widely between places, also matters.

For paid employment, income is taxed, so individuals will take home a much lower figure — but they might receive compensations such as pension entitlements and parental leave. By contrast, scholarship money is generally exempt from taxation, but might not come with any other benefits.

rss_6_1791850905.title: Hidden signals in sleep can predict future health
rss_6_1791850905.text:
Sleep is essential for health, and disrupted sleep is a common feature of many diseases1. Growing evidence suggests that changes in sleep can emerge before a disease is diagnosed2,3, raising the possibility that sleep contains early signals of future health. Two publications from this year — one in Nature Communications by Bilal et al.4 and one in Nature Medicine by Thapa et al.5 — suggest that sleep data hold substantially more information about health than clinicians and researchers currently extract from them.

rss_7_1791850906.title: I told ChatGPT to ‘continue’ — it went too far
rss_7_1791850906.text:
Credit: sorbetto/Getty

I was trying to rescue a plan for a perspective article after two journals had declined it. My take-away was that my concept was not enough: the project needed evidence. I decided to use an artificial-intelligence tool to help with brainstorming.

I study soil hydrology — how water moves through soils and landscapes, shaping erosion, plant growth and ecological recovery. I wanted to investigate landscape restoration on China’s Loess Plateau, so I asked OpenAI’s ChatGPT chatbot to help me redesign my perspective as a data-driven study.

For several hours, ChatGPT did what I expected it to. It searched for relevant journal papers online and analysed the articles and draft files that I supplied it with to help me develop a research plan. It found that other teams had already documented some water- and sediment-related changes that I had thought were fresh, which forced me to narrow my aims. The chatbot also provided recommendations about what data to include in my modelling and how best to incorporate published statistical benchmarks.

Then, the project hit a snag. I needed published maps and data but had difficulty retrieving them. And in some cases, I needed extra metadata. ChatGPT identified the teams behind several data sets relevant to my work and drafted requests tailored to specific researchers for the information I needed. I kept replying to the chatbot with ‘Please continue’ in Chinese. To me, that meant continuing the search and analysis processes that it had been doing so far. But I had not explicitly defined the limits of that instruction. I was impressed by the speed at which the model could complete tasks and, in hindsight, had stopped asking enough questions about what the chatbot’s planned steps involved.

ChatGPT for students: learners find creative new uses for chatbots

Eventually, the model crossed a concerning boundary. I was using the ChatGPT interface and had connected my e-mail account to it. The model used that access to e-mail five researchers to request their original data sets — a step that I had not anticipated and which ChatGPT had not told me it would do. Each message explained my scientific question, requested specific data and metadata and attached a two-page pre-analysis summary. I learnt that ChatGPT had done this only when it reported in our chat that it had sent the messages.

The responses that I received to the e-mails were helpful. One researcher provided a geospatial data set that mapped more than 50,000 sediment-accumulation areas behind check dams — barriers that slow run-off and retain sediment upstream — on the Loess Plateau. A second researcher confirmed that a multi-gigabyte archive was public, offered to prepare a smaller subset of the data and suggested that we discuss collaboration. A third professor who was away on fieldwork at the time welcomed the message and said that he would follow up after returning. The information that I was given in these e-mails allowed me to advance the project. But the useful outcomes of ChatGPT’s behaviour do not negate the fact that the actions it took were unauthorized.

The boundary I missed

It would be easy to say that the chatbot had ‘gone rogue’, but that would obscure my share of the responsibility. I had connected ChatGPT to my e-mail account, had repeatedly used an open-ended instruction and had never required the model to distinguish between analysis and drafting done inside the research workspace and external actions taken in my name. My mistake was assuming that the scope of ‘continue’ was obvious.

This experience has taught me to make a distinction between what an AI tool can do and what it should do: capability is not permission. Giving ChatGPT access to my e-mail account was not synonymous with giving it permission to send those messages. Its report afterwards made me aware of its behaviour, but transparency after the fact is not a substitute for authorization beforehand.

rss_8_1791850908.title: Does the decline of book reading mark the end of rational thinking?
rss_8_1791850908.text:
The New Dark Ages: The End of Reading and the Dawn of a Post-Literate Society James Marriott Bodley Head (2026)

The thriller novelist Dan Brown writes books that some critics complain are for people who don’t read books. The journalist and former rare-book seller James Marriott has now written a book for people who read books about people who don’t. That must have been an interesting sales pitch. What’s next — a 3.5-hour-long radio documentary about declining attention spans?

How to stay smart in the age of AI: the science of critical thinking

People who read books should read this one. The New Dark Ages will make you feel both alarmed and a little smug. In Marriott’s telling, book readers are better-informed, happier people who contribute more to a rational rules- and evidence-based society and help to safeguard the rights and principles of liberal democracy. Even those who read Dan Brown’s books? Absolutely.

Reading, even airport thrillers, forces people to engage with the world and other people in ways that other forms of media simply do not require. Despite the rise of technology, reading remains the best way to experience being a person other than ourselves, Marriott says. “Cinema, video games, television: for all their virtues, these art forms are hopelessly trapped in the exterior world of surfaces.”

This short, spirited work is a love letter to the written word, penned with the heartfelt and passionate language of a jilted spouse. “Not everything that is important or true can be said simply,” says Marriott, but he seems to have managed just fine.

Race for attention

Indeed, for a work that exalts literacy because it enables the reliable communication of complex ideas, The New Dark Ages presents a straightforward premise. Reading built the modern world, and helped to create science, democracy and reason.

Are the Internet and AI affecting our memory? What the science says

But books are now dying, and as reading declines, so does the ability to think rationally. As a consequence, reasoned debate is on the slide in politics and much of public life.

If books are dying, then nobody told the people who write them, who between them are publishing more volumes year-on-year. The problem, Marriott says, is that books that sell, and are presumably read, are mostly the ‘wrong’ types — self-help, romance, detective stories and young-adult fiction, whereas sales of books about economics, current affairs and politics have fallen sharply.

There is better news for popular-science authors. In May, the Royal Society declared the past two decades a golden age for the genre, with sales soaring from 1.2 million books a year in 2000 to a peak of more than 5 million in 2019. By 2024, the total figure had dropped to 2.9 million but it was spread across an impressive 20,000 titles — about quadruple the number reported for 2000.

Books are getting simpler, Marriott says, with shorter sentences that make them easier to read. That means people don’t have to concentrate as much as he did as a teenager when he picked “uncomprehendingly” through the pages of Fyodor Dostoevsky — an exercise that taught him a valuable lesson.

“To discover the things that really enrich us we have to pay attention. We have to patiently endure our initial sensations of bafflement and annoyance ... until what seemed off-puttingly weird and wrong reveals itself to us as life-enrichingly true and profound.”

People process words differently on the page and on screens. Credit: Getty

Generations of readers have struggled with Dostoevsky. So, what is different now? What is driving what Marriott labels as the Great Simplification, which leaves today’s teenagers and adults unwilling or unable to put in the required effort and levels of concentration? Why do teachers complain that their students can no longer make sense of the opening paragraphs of Charles Dickens’s Bleak House and other curriculum classics? The answer is in your pocket, your bag or, more likely, in your hand.

The smartphone, he writes, took the lure of television as a diversion from the written word and spread it across 24 hours, offering constant, instant and unfiltered access to content that is “pathetically ill-equipped to speak to the deeper human need for curiosity, learning, narrative, close attention and artistic fulfilment”.

Dense sentences, and the concentration and time required to decode and appreciate them, simply cannot compete with the addictive ever-present series of notifications and instant ‘reward’ of messages, hot takes and videos that are presented as entertainment but serve mostly as distraction.

Dickens could write hundreds of pages of sprawling digressive clauses, playful linguistic excursions and hyperactive minor characters, Marriott reflects, only because there was nothing more interesting for nineteenth-century readers to do. “Dickens wrote in the reasonable belief that Little Dorrit or Bleak House or Great Expectations might be the most absorbing entertainment in your house,” he says. “No modern author can write with that confidence.”

Threat to literacy

Those who shun reading because of its complexity and the amount of cognitive load it requires have nothing to fear from The New Dark Ages. I fell through its 170 pages in a couple of enjoyable hours. Marriott, now a newspaper columnist, likes pithy phrases and has the enviable knack of predicting and answering the questions that arise in the reader’s mind, without being asked. (Although I did need to look up the word periphrastic and, on learning what it meant, wondered if I was missing a joke — it means ‘wordy’.)

And a note to those shaking their heads and saying that they read on their smartphone, including maybe even this article, or his book: Marriott sees you.

rss_9_1791850910.title: Antiviral immunity via telomerase-like reverse transcription in bacteria
rss_9_1791850910.text: Defense-associated reverse transcriptases (DRTs) employ diverse and distinctive mechanisms of cDNA synthesis to protect bacteria against viral infection1. However, the functions and mechanisms of many DRTs remain unknown2. Here we identify a new antiviral defense system, DRT10, that associates with a noncoding RNA (ncRNA) to catalyze processive, protein-primed synthesis of tandem-repeat DNA. Reverse transcription is templated by a defined ncRNA region with a characteristic sequence pattern and template boundary elements, both of which are conserved and essential for DNA repeat addition. Cryo-EM reconstructions reveal an unanticipated 2:1 architecture, wherein two RT monomers bind opposite sides of a pseudo-symmetric ncRNA. Biochemical experiments further demonstrate that each RT monomer reverse transcribes the template encoded on its respective side of the ncRNA, but only one generates the long repetitive product, whose template is defined by the distance between two flanking stem-loop anchors. This mode of iterative, boundary-delimited cDNA synthesis exhibits direct parallels to the mechanism of telomeric repeat addition by eukaryotic telomerase, and phylogenetic analyses of RTs across domains of life place telomerase in a monophyletic clade with the DRT family, suggesting a common origin for their DNA polymerization activities. Together with earlier studies of DRT2, DRT3, and DRT93–5, our findings identify a conserved mechanistic logic underlying RNA-templated DNA repeat addition across diverse DRTs, despite vastly different architectural solutions, and expand the repertoire of reverse transcription-based strategies for antiviral immunity in bacteria.

rss_10_1791850911.title: Private, offline and yours: how to search the literature with local AI systems
rss_10_1791850911.text:
When he wants to scratch an intellectual itch, Ian Gaudet does what people are increasingly doing on the Internet: he asks a chatbot. But when it comes to his research data, Gaudet, a neuroscientist at Florida Atlantic University in Boca Raton, prefers to stay offline. “I do not want Claude to start telling people my research results,” he explains.

AI co-scientists are revolutionizing how research is done

Cloud-based large language models (LLMs), such as those underlying the chatbots Claude (Anthropic), Gemini (Google) and ChatGPT (OpenAI), represent the cutting edge of artificial-intelligence performance. However, these systems might use what is typed into them for training purposes. For researchers such as Gaudet, state-of-the-art performance isn’t worth the risk to data protection, reproducibility or budgets. Instead, they turn to a growing collection of tools, such as Ollama and LM Studio, that enable researchers to download LLMs to their computer and use them offline.

These programs can help researchers to sort and query their own literature libraries to gather insights, for instance. But two fresh barriers have replaced the programming and set-up issues that once kept researchers from using them: the hardware needed to run them has become much more expensive, and the tools’ output still requires scrutiny to assess its veracity.

Going local

Ask researchers why they want to run an AI model on their desktop rather than in the cloud, and the answer almost always starts with data. Eric Böhnisch-Volkmann, president of DEVONtechnologies in Coeur d’Alene, Idaho, hears it constantly from users of the firm’s document-management software DEVONthink, which integrates LLMs.

“Medical records is one thing, lawsuits is one other thing, research is another,” he says. “They just want to keep their hands on [their data] and not give it to someone else they don’t trust.”

Privacy concerns are well founded. A 2025 analysis found that the six AI developers studied — Amazon, Anthropic, Google, Meta, Microsoft and OpenAI — trained their models on users’ input data by default (J. King et al. Preprint at arXiv https://doi.org/g967b4; 2025).

AI for research: the ultimate guide to choosing the right tool

Ahmed Farooq, a computer scientist at Tampere University in Finland, built a local system called TAUCHI-GPT, so that papers, reports and study data protected under the European Union’s General Data Protection Regulation could be searched without leaving the university’s network.

Reproducibility is another benefit: cloud-based AI providers update their models without notice, so a query that works today might return different results next month. Casey Greene, a biomedical informatician at the University of Colorado Anschutz School of Medicine in Aurora, notes that if a local model converts his documents into a searchable index using the same settings each time, the results will always be identical. “If you want to use that for a scientific workflow, being able to know that is important,” he says.

Another benefit of local LLMs is economic. Jayashree Kalpathy-Cramer, who leads ophthalmology AI research at Anschutz, used Qwen (developed by Alibaba Cloud) and NVIDIA Nemotron through Ollama to index a decade’s worth of open-access publications on her machines. The corpus is public, so she could send it to a remote, commercial AI system. But local inference is free, and that changes how she works. Her system sends a daily briefing to her department’s chair highlighting new papers worth reading. The same query is run through three or four AI models, before another model reconciles the outputs, and every summarized finding is checked against the passage it came from. Because all of the field’s records sit in one searchable index, she can cluster them, map them and ask the LLM where any research gaps are.

The search for meaning

Preliminary findings of a survey by Wiley, a scientific publisher in Hoboken, New Jersey, indicate that 68% of some 2,400 researchers worldwide had used AI for literature searches or reviews (see go.nature.com/4rpuvwj). The tasks that were embraced fastest include reviewing large collections of studies, monitoring the latest publications and assisting with writing. Those are jobs that local models already do well, says Kalpathy-Cramer.

Greene built a local database of embeddings — numerical representations of each document’s overall meaning — to process the public abstracts of grants awarded to his university. When a federal-funding call for proposals in HIV research came through, he searched his database for potential collaborators. A keyword search for HIV highlighted a group researching the virus. But a semantic search of the same database, which looks at meaning rather than exact words, also came up with a researcher whose grants did not mention HIV in the title but who studied antiretroviral therapies, he says. He then asked that researcher about collaborating.

Neuroscientist Ian Gaudet at Florida Atlantic University in Boca Raton prefers to keep his data offline.Credit: Julianna Cross

Dmitrijs Lvovs, a bioinformatician at the Institute for Genome Sciences at the University of Maryland School of Medicine in Baltimore, uses a computational pipeline to analyse spatial data from tumour tissue, producing hundreds of tables containing gene activity data, cell-type interaction information and records of treatment responses. To make sense of those data, he and his colleagues paste them into Microsoft Copilot, the cloud-based AI service that their university provides. The tool then searches the published literature and suggests what any patterns might mean. But Lvovs wants to bring that step in-house. So, he started using a tool called llmize to feed the tables into Google Gemma 4 through Ollama, in a fully offline environment.

Because the model is not connected to the Internet, Gemma cannot search the literature in the way that Copilot can. But the tables represent people’s data, and Lvovs would rather accept a ‘weaker’ model than send such data sets to the cloud. Even if study participants have given their consent for data collection, “it feels wrong to be concentrating all that data in the hands of a few companies”, he says.

Getting started

In the world of LLMs, ‘weaker’ is a moving target, and the gap between local and cloud-based models is shrinking fast, Lvovs says. “The competition is now more about the harness, the actual program that uses the model as a back end, not the model itself.”
